newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Rosy Brazil data not seen heralding strong growth.
newsitem.headline: Rosy Brazil data not seen heralding strong growth.

text.p: Figures released this week show Brazilian industrial activity and jobs growth are at their best levels in two years, but economists say the numbers do not point to a trend of heightened economic activity.
Rather, economists say the latest figures distort the economy's true performance and most are ratcheting down their 1997 economic growth forecasts to around 3.0-3.5 percent from 3.5-4.0 percent.
Brazilian industrial output in April rose 7.9 percent year-on-year, the best result since April 1995, according to the government's National Statistics Institute (IBGE).
Also, for the first time since March 1995, Sao Paulo State Industries Federation (Fiesp) reported that hirings at Sao Paulo private firms surpassed dismissals.
Economists said strong industrial output in April, however, was as much a reflection of the month's greater number of working days as it was of stepped-up economic activity.
"April figures may be overstated because there were more working days than in March," said Denise Paschoal, an economist at counsulting firm Trend Analise.
In addition, greater-than-expected jobs growth in May does not reverse a trend in Brazil toward diminishing industrial employment, economists said.
"The trend continues to be a reduction in job offers," said Jose Mauro Dellela, economist at Lloyds Bank, Brazil.
Fiesp reported that 550 industrial jobs were added in the state of Sao Paulo in May, reversing a 25-month trend of job losses in the state.
Dellela and other analysts, who said the jobs gain was too small to reflect a trend, said private firms would continue cutting staff as part of ongoing company restructurings and modernization.
He said the Brazilian economy continues to grow by sector, with durable and construction goods sailing ahead, while textile and capital goods improving at a slower pace.

Brazilian policy-makers say they are content with the current pace of growth, realizing they do not want to spur the economy amid a burgeoning current account gap, expected to top $30 billion this year.
In fact, Brazil's deteriorating trade balance, the prime contributor to the current account gap, could prompt the government to adopt further credit restrictions to slow the economy.
"I don't think it is likely to happen now, but I cannot rule out that possibility in the future," Dellela said.

Last month, Brazil moved to curb consumption by increasing a financial tax on credit in a bid to cut the country's widening trade gap. That move followed import financing restrictions, which were imposed in March to discourage imports.
So far this year, Brazil's trade deficit totals $4.2 billion, and analysts predict it will reach $10 billion to $11 billion by the end of the year.
